passage:
I sit next to Yogesh in Class 5, so I notice a lot. When our teacher split us into teams for the quiz, he told Mohit, "You want to be the writer, right? You like neat handwriting. I'll do the buzzer." That was new. Last year he just grabbed every job.
But on Friday Mohit said he'd miss Sunday's cricket match for his cousin's birthday. Yogesh's ears went red. "You're only saying that because you don't care about the team." He kicked his bag all the way to the gate.
I don't know what he was thinking. Maybe he just wanted to win really badly.
— Swati

qa.q: What job did Yogesh suggest Mohit take in the quiz?
qa.a: The writer, because Mohit likes neat handwriting.

qa.q: Why might Yogesh have felt so sure Mohit didn't care about the team?
qa.a: Yogesh felt angry and disappointed because he wanted the match so badly that a different, fair reason was hard for him to imagine.

qa.q: What could help Yogesh at a moment like Friday's?
qa.a: Taking a breath and asking Mohit about the birthday before answering could let him hear the reason before deciding what it means.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when Yogesh says he doesn't care about the team?
qa.a: Mohit may feel hurt and unfairly judged, since he only wanted to be at his cousin's birthday 😔

grounding: A classmate sees a ten-year-old boy read a friend's wishes well in a calm moment but lose that view when his own wish is strong.

passage:
Sunday. Jomon lent Avni his favourite comic and waited all week for her to say it was the best. She handed it back. "It was okay. I like mystery ones more." Jomon blinked, then nodded. "Oh. Different taste, I guess."
Wednesday. They had to pick a science fair topic. Jomon had set his heart on volcanoes. Avni wanted plants. "Plants are boring! Nobody wants plants!" he shouted, and walked off.
Saturday. He turned up at her gate with two sheets of paper. "I write volcano facts, you write plant facts. Then we pick."
Avni laughed. "Or we do plants that grow near volcanoes."

qa.q: What topic did Avni want for the science fair?
qa.a: Plants.

qa.q: Why did Jomon shout that nobody wants plants?
qa.a: Jomon had set his heart on volcanoes, and that strong wish made it feel as if everyone must want the same, even though on Sunday he'd accepted that Avni's tastes differ.

qa.q: Which choice on Saturday helped Jomon and Avni move forward?
qa.a: Jomon brought two sheets so each could list facts for their own topic before choosing, which gave Avni's idea a fair hearing.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt on Wednesday when Jomon walked off?
qa.a: Avni was probably hurt and puzzled, since only days before he had calmly accepted that she likes different comics.

grounding: Over a week, a boy who accepts a friend's different taste in comics struggles when he badly wants his own science topic, then finds a fairer way.

passage:
Sit, Naveen. You're sulking because your friend picked the other team, so let your old Uncle Farhan tell you something.
When I was ten, my best friend Iqbal and I saved coins for one kite to share. I knew he liked green. I liked red. At the shop I even told the man, "He'll want the green one." I was proud of knowing that.
We had enough for only one. Iqbal picked green. I was so angry I told him he'd done it on purpose to spoil my day. He hadn't. He simply liked green, and I knew it.
It took me two days to go back to his house. We flew the green kite together. It flew very well.

qa.q: Which colour kite did Iqbal pick?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: Why did young Farhan believe Iqbal picked green on purpose?
qa.a: Farhan badly wanted red, and that disappointment made Iqbal's choice feel aimed at him, even though he already knew Iqbal simply liked green.

qa.q: What choice turned things around after two days?
qa.a: Farhan went back to Iqbal's house and they flew the green kite together, letting the friendship matter more than the colour.

qa.q: How might Naveen see the friend's team choice after hearing this story?
qa.a: Naveen may start to see it as a different wish rather than a betrayal, just as Farhan came to see Iqbal's choice of green.

grounding: An uncle recalls how at ten he knew his friend's likes yet still felt betrayed when his own strong wish was blocked.

passage: Only forty minutes before the Jayanagar library closed, and Mridul, ten, and Sumit still hadn't picked a book for their project. "You want the planets one, I know," Mridul said. "You think dinosaurs are for babies. Fine, planets." He felt proud; last year he'd have just grabbed dinosaurs. Then Sumit said, "For the next project, I'm pairing with Farhan. He's good at drawing." Mridul's face went hot. "So you think I'm useless." "I didn't say that." "You meant it." Mridul stomped to the checkout. The lights flicked, the guard called closing time, and Sumit stood holding the planets book, looking confused.

qa.q: How long was it before the library closed?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Mridul decide Sumit thought he was useless?
qa.a: His hurt at not being picked for the next project was so strong that he read his own feeling into Sumit's words.

qa.q: What could Mridul try the next time a hot feeling like that comes?
qa.a: He could pause and ask Sumit what was meant, the same way he had guessed Sumit's wish for the planets book.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt holding the planets book?
qa.a: Sumit probably felt confused and hurt, since a simple plan about drawing turned into being accused of something never said.

grounding: Under time pressure, a boy correctly reads what a friend wants but misjudges the friend's meaning once his own feelings are hurt.

passage: Hrithik, eleven, was proud of the plan. Pankaj's birthday surprise was set for Saturday in their Kolkata colony hall, and Pankaj had no idea. "He thinks we forgot," Hrithik whispered to the others. "So act normal." On Saturday Pankaj walked in, gasped and laughed. Hrithik handed over his present: a new football, the thing Hrithik wanted most in the world. Pankaj smiled politely. "Thanks... I'll use it." Then his eyes lit up at a book from his cousin. Hrithik's chest went tight. "Everyone loves football," he muttered to his mother at home. "He's just pretending not to." She asked, "Does Pankaj play much?" Hrithik went quiet. "He mostly reads," he admitted, still sulking.

qa.q: Where was Pankaj's surprise held?
qa.a: In their Kolkata colony hall.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik insist that Pankaj was only pretending not to love football?
qa.a: He was disappointed that his gift wasn't loved, and his strong feelings made it hard to accept that Pankaj simply wants different things.

qa.q: What question helped Hrithik think again, and what might he do next time?
qa.a: His mother asking "Does Pankaj play much?"; next time he could think about what Pankaj enjoys before choosing a gift.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt opening the football?
qa.a: Pankaj probably felt grateful for the thought but not excited, and tried to be polite so as not to hurt Hrithik.

grounding: A boy understands his friend doesn't know about a surprise, but struggles to accept the friend wants different things when his own feelings are involved.

passage: Farhan, you're angry your friend chose someone else for his team? Listen to your Akash Nana. When I was nine, in Jabalpur, my best friend Prakash wanted a kite for his birthday. I wanted to give him marbles, because I loved marbles. But then I thought, no, Prakash loves kites, not marbles. So I bought a kite. I was so proud of that thought! Then, one month later, Prakash picked a new boy, Salim, as his partner for the school sports. I was furious. I told everyone Prakash was a traitor. I couldn't think at all why he'd do it. Only later I learnt Salim was new and had no friends. Prakash was being kind. I had understood the kite. I couldn't understand the partner, because I was too hurt to think.

qa.q: What did Prakash want for his birthday?
qa.a: A kite.

qa.q: Why couldn't young Akash see why Prakash chose Salim?
qa.a: He felt hurt and furious, and his strong feelings blocked him from thinking about what Prakash might want, even though he had understood the kite.

qa.q: What choice in the story could Akash have made differently when Prakash picked Salim?
qa.a: He could have asked Prakash why before calling him a traitor, which would have shown him Prakash was being kind to a new boy.

qa.q: How might Salim have felt being chosen as a partner?
qa.a: Salim, new and without friends, likely felt relieved and welcomed when Prakash picked him.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a child beginning to see that a friend wants different things, but struggling when his own strong feelings take over.

passage: The picnic was cancelled because of the rain, and Anand and his sister Tanuja were stuck in the flat all Saturday with one TV. Anand wanted cricket highlights. Tanuja wanted her cartoon. "Fine," Anand said, surprising himself. "You watch first. You've been waiting all week for that episode." Tanuja stared at him. He felt quite grown-up. Then, at four, the match started live, and Tanuja asked for just ten more minutes. Anand's face went hot. "You always get your way!" he shouted, and snatched the remote. Tanuja cried. Anand stood there, remote in hand, knowing somewhere inside that she had only asked for ten minutes. He couldn't make himself give it back. Not yet.

qa.q: Why was the picnic cancelled?
qa.a: Because of the rain.

qa.q: Why could Anand see what Tanuja wanted in the morning but not at four?
qa.a: In the morning he felt calm and grown-up, so he could think about her wishes; when the live match started, his strong excitement and frustration swamped that understanding.

qa.q: What could Anand try next time his feelings get very strong?
qa.a: He could take a breath and remember what he did in the morning, or suggest a fair plan like taking turns every half hour.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel when Anand snatches the remote after being kind earlier?
qa.a: She probably feels hurt and confused, since he had just been so fair to her.

grounding: Shows an older child beginning to understand his sister wants different things, but losing that understanding when his own strong feelings take over.

passage: In the colony lane in Kochi, Gautam heard Thomas telling everyone the zoo trip was on Tuesday. Gautam knew it had moved to Thursday. He thought, Thomas doesn't know; he wasn't there when Ma'am said it. So he told him. Thomas thanked him. Gautam felt clever. Later, at the lane cricket match, Thomas asked to bowl first. Gautam wanted to bowl first too. He had been practising his spin all week. "No, you always bowl first!" Gautam shouted, though Thomas never did. Thomas walked off. That night Gautam lay in bed. He could see now that Thomas just wanted a turn, like him. Why hadn't he seen it at the time?

qa.q: What day did the zoo trip move to?
qa.a: Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel clever about telling Thomas the trip date?
qa.a: He felt proud because he understood that Thomas believed something different since he hadn't heard the teacher.

qa.q: What could Gautam do tomorrow to make things right with Thomas?
qa.a: He could say sorry for shouting and suggest taking turns to bowl first.

qa.q: If you were Thomas, what would you want Gautam to understand?
qa.a: That he only wanted a turn at bowling, and it hurt to be told he always bowled first when he never did.

grounding: Shows an older child understanding that a friend believes different things, but struggling when his own strong wish to bowl takes over.

passage:
"Kishore, why did you give Uday a football for his birthday? He doesn't even play."

"Because I love football, Ma."

"But what does Uday love?"

"...Drawing, I think."

"So?"

"So maybe he'd like colours more." Kishore frowned. "But football is the best present."

"For you."

Kishore sighed. "I get it. People like different things."

Later, Uday opened the football and said politely, "Thanks." Kishore saw his face and felt his cheeks burn.

"Next time I'll ask what you like," he muttered.

Uday grinned. "Colours. Always colours."

qa.q: What does Uday love?
qa.a: Drawing.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he saw Uday's face?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his cheeks burning, realising Uday didn't love the football.

qa.q: What could Kishore do next time he buys a present?
qa.a: Ask what the friend likes, or think about what they enjoy, instead of what he likes.

qa.q: How might Uday feel opening the football?
qa.a: Uday probably felt a bit disappointed but polite, not wanting to hurt Kishore.

grounding: An older child begins to see that friends want different things but struggles when his own strong feelings are involved.

passage:
Last year my friend Manoj and I both wanted to be captain of the class cricket team. I thought, obviously I should be captain. I'm the best bowler.

When Manoj got picked, I was so angry I didn't talk to him for two days. I thought he knew how much I wanted it, and he took it anyway.

Then Ma asked me, "Did Manoj want it too?" I said yes. "So he felt the same as you." I hadn't thought of that.

I understand now that people can want the same thing and it's not about me. But when I'm upset, it's still hard to remember.

I'm Siddharth. I talk to Manoj again. He lets me bowl first.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth expect to be made captain?
qa.a: Siddharth thought being the best bowler made it obvious.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when Manoj was picked?
qa.a: Siddharth felt angry and hurt, thinking Manoj knew and took it anyway.

qa.q: What question helped Siddharth see Manoj's view?
qa.a: Ma asked, "Did Manoj want it too?", which showed they both felt the same.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt during the two days of silence?
qa.a: Manoj probably felt hurt and confused, since he just wanted to be captain too.

grounding: An older child begins to understand friends want different things but struggles when strong feelings are involved.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5, Monday.

Ramesh understands a lot about others now. In story time, he can explain why a character feels jealous or scared. But today, when his friend Bhupen chose to sit with a new boy at lunch, Ramesh said loudly, "He doesn't like me anymore."

I asked him, "Is there another reason Bhupen might sit there?"

Ramesh thought. "Maybe to be kind to the new boy." Then he added, "But he should sit with me."

He can see others' views when he's calm, but it's harder when he feels hurt. I'll keep asking these questions gently, and I've paired him with Bhupen for the project this week.

qa.q: Who did Bhupen sit with at lunch?
qa.a: A new boy.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh say "He doesn't like me anymore"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and jealous, and those strong feelings made it hard to see Bhupen's reason.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to help Ramesh?
qa.a: The teacher asked if Bhupen might have another reason and paired them for the project.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel if he heard Ramesh's comment?
qa.a: Bhupen might feel sad or confused, since he was only being kind to the new boy.

grounding: A teacher notes an older child who understands others' views when calm but struggles when his own feelings are strong.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Diwali holidays, day two. At the rangoli competition, Zainab wanted to use blue and I wanted orange. I said, "Okay, you like blue, I like orange, that's allowed." I felt very grown-up! Then her team won the prize and ours didn't, and I said she cheated. I KNEW she didn't. I just felt so bad inside that it came out. Mumma said, "You understood she likes blue. Can you also understand she's happy, even if you're sad?" I'm trying. It's harder when I'm upset. Tomorrow I'll say sorry to Zainab.
Baljeet

qa.q: What colour did Zainab want to use?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet say Zainab cheated?
qa.a: Baljeet felt so bad and disappointed about losing that the feeling came out as an accusation, even while knowing she hadn't cheated.

qa.q: What is Baljeet planning, and why is it right?
qa.a: To say sorry to Zainab tomorrow, owning the unfair words said while upset.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel being called a cheat?
qa.a: She would likely feel hurt and confused, especially on a day she was happy about winning.

grounding: A child understands a friend can want different things, but struggles to hold that view when upset.

passage: On Sankranti morning in the village, Divyansh and his friend Elizabeth flew kites from the flat roof. "You want the high wind, I want the low," Divyansh said, proud he had noticed. "Different wants." Then Elizabeth's kite cut his string, and his red kite drifted away over the fields. His face went hot. "You did that on purpose! You wanted my kite gone!" Elizabeth stared. "I didn't even see it." Somewhere inside, Divyansh knew she was telling the truth. But the angry feeling was so big that it drowned out the knowing. He stomped downstairs, then stopped on the last step.

qa.q: What colour was Divyansh's kite?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh accuse Elizabeth though part of him knew she was honest?
qa.a: He felt hot, angry and upset about losing his kite, and the big feeling drowned out his understanding that she had her own view.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do next?
qa.a: Take a breath on the step, go back and say he knows she didn't mean it, and perhaps fly a kite together.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when accused?
qa.a: Shocked and hurt, since she hadn't even seen his kite.

grounding: A child who understands friends want different things still struggles to see a friend's view when he is upset.

passage: During the summer holidays in Guadalajara, Alejandro hid Sofia's ball in the laundry basket while she was inside. "She'll look in the garden," he told his cousin, grinning. "Because she doesn't know I moved it." He was proud of that thought. But when Sofia came out and looked straight in the basket, he shouted, "You peeked! You knew!" Sofia shrugged. "It's always there." Alejandro's cheeks burned. He wanted to win so much that he couldn't believe she had simply guessed. Later, calmer, he admitted, "Maybe you just thought of it."

qa.q: Where did Alejandro hide Sofia's ball?
qa.a: In the laundry basket.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro accuse Sofia of peeking?
qa.a: He wanted to win so badly that frustration and embarrassment stopped him believing she had simply guessed.

qa.q: What could help Alejandro in games like this?
qa.a: Pausing when his cheeks start burning, and reminding himself that others have their own reasons, like "it's always there".

qa.q: How does Sofia see the moment?
qa.a: She seems calm, even puzzled, since for her the basket was simply the obvious place.

grounding: A child understands a friend has different knowledge, but struggles when the wish to win takes over.

passage: On the first frosty morning of winter football camp, Harsha and Francis were picking positions. Francis wanted to be goalkeeper. Harsha hated standing in goal and used to think everyone did. "Okay, you like the gloves, I get it," Harsha said, handing them over. By the second half, though, Harsha's side was losing three–nil and the coach moved Harsha back to defence. "Francis, swap with me. You'd rather be out here, obviously!" Francis shook his head. "I told you, I like goal." Harsha kicked the white grass. "Nobody likes standing in goal when we're losing." Francis just pulled the gloves tighter and faced the pitch.

qa.q: Which position did Francis want to play?
qa.a: Francis wanted to be goalkeeper.

qa.q: Why did Harsha insist that Francis would rather swap?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and embarrassed about losing, and that strong feeling pushed him back into assuming Francis must want what he wanted.

qa.q: What could Harsha try next time he is upset during a match?
qa.a: Take a breath and ask "Do you still want goal?" instead of deciding for Francis; his own feelings can be real without being Francis's too.

qa.q: How does Francis feel when Harsha tells him what he would rather do?
qa.a: He likely feels unheard and a bit annoyed, since he had already said he likes goal; pulling the gloves tighter shows he is holding his ground.

grounding: An older child accepts that a friend wants something different, but slips back into assuming his own wants when losing makes his feelings strong.
